zones.name: Buying territory from a state
zones.who_owns: The selling state holds sovereignty until a treaty moves it to the buyer.

rules.says: Lists transfers of sovereignty by agreement in which money was paid, and every buyer and seller listed is a state or a state-like ruler. Leases are excluded.
The decision on Greenland's independence belongs to the Greenlandic people, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum in Greenland.

zones.hook: The government that holds the land can refuse to sell, as Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly done. A buyer who is not a state has no treaty partner to hand sovereignty over.
zones.can_you_build: Open talks with a government that would give up sovereignty over part of its land. The only private attempt verified here, Anton Bakov's Romanov Empire, reported unsuccessful talks with Kiribati and the Gambia as of 2017.
facts: Louisiana: $15m, 1803, 2,140,000 km²
Danish West Indies: $25m, 1916, 400 km²
Latest purchase on the list: Gwadar, £3m, 1958

sources.t: List of territory purchased by a sovereign nation from another sovereign nation

zones.name: Leases and extraterritorial spots
zones.who_owns: The host state usually keeps ultimate sovereignty. Another state or body runs the place under a lease, treaty or diplomatic rule.

rules.cite: Treaty between Malta and the Order of Malta, 1998
rules.says: Gives the Order the upper part of Fort St Angelo with limited extraterritoriality for 99 years. Malta may end it at any time after 50 years.
Ending the lease needs consent from both sides or full US military withdrawal.
These zones are fully under the jurisdiction of the country where they sit, and local law applies inside them.

zones.hook: The host can end a term-limited lease, or the occupant can invite the police in, as Ecuador did in 2019. Airports stay under national law throughout, so staying there gives no separate status.
zones.can_you_build: A lease has been granted only to a state or a state-like body in the cases found here. A private person can reach this kind of place only as a guest of that body, as an asylum seeker in an embassy or a stranded traveller.
facts: Guantanamo: 117 km², rent $4,085 a year, one cheque cashed since 1959
New Territories: 99 years, rent-free, 235 islands, expired 30 June 1997
Panama Canal Zone: 1,432 km², 1903–1979
Assange: nearly seven years inside a suite of rooms in a London flat block
Nasseri: about 18 years in Terminal 1

sources.t: Convention for the Extension of Hong Kong Territory

zones.name: Places run by international agreement
zones.who_owns: Whoever the treaty names: the League of Nations, the UN Security Council, a committee of foreign powers, or two states jointly.

rules.says: Created the Free City of Danzig under League of Nations protection.

rules.cite: UN Security Council Resolution 16 and the 1947 Treaty of Peace with Italy
rules.says: Set up the Free Territory of Trieste under Security Council responsibility.
Placed Kosovo under UN administration from 1999.

zones.hook: These places exist only while the powers that signed keep agreeing. Danzig was annexed in 1939, Trieste was split in 1954, Tangier was abolished by its protecting powers, and Jerusalem's plan was never carried out.
zones.can_you_build: A person cannot start one. It takes a treaty or a UN decision, usually as a way to settle a dispute between states after a war.
facts: Tangier: 373 km², 1923–1956
Danzig: 1,952 km², 366,730 people in 1923
Trieste lasted seven years and never received its governor
Brčko District: 493 km², 83,516 people, created 8 March 2000

zones.name: Buffer zones and no-go strips
zones.who_owns: The surrounding states or armistice parties keep their claims. A peacekeeping force or armistice body controls entry.

rules.says: Each side moved back 2,000 metres from the front line, creating a zone about 4 km wide.
Patrolled by the UN force in Cyprus and extended after the 16 August 1974 ceasefire.

zones.hook: Soldiers and entry permits control access. In the Korean zone only two villages are allowed to remain, and Chernobyl's exclusion zone is cordoned off, with self-settlers living there without official permission.
zones.can_you_build: No declared state in such a zone was found. People live in them as prior residents or their descendants, and they remain citizens of an existing state.
facts: Cyprus zone: 346 km², 180 km long, about 10,000 residents
Korean DMZ: about 250 km by 4 km; Tae Sung Dong had 218 people in 2008
Chernobyl: about 1,200 returned in 1986; 135 left in 2017

sources.t: United Nations Buffer Zone in Cyprus

zones.name: Secession by referendum or decolonisation
zones.who_owns: The existing state, unless it agrees to let go or loses control.

rules.says: A state needs a defined territory, a permanent population, a government and the capacity to deal with other states.

rules.cite: International Court of Justice, Kosovo advisory opinion, 22 July 2010
rules.says: By 10 votes to 4, found Kosovo's declaration of independence did not violate international law.
Suspended Catalonia's referendum law and later declared it void.

zones.hook: The parent state can refuse consent, send police or soldiers, take over the regional government or fight a war. Without its consent, recognition from other states tends to stay limited.
zones.can_you_build: Win a mandate inside the territory, then get the parent state to agree to a binding vote. South Sudan, Montenegro and Eritrea all voted under agreed terms and were widely accepted afterwards.
facts: Own count of Wikipedia's referendum table as retrieved in November 2026: of about 123 votes parsed, 31 led to a recognised independent state, 12 to de facto control with no or partial recognition, 16 to a yes vote with no independence, and 59 to a no vote
South Sudan: 98.83% yes
Eritrea: 99.83% yes
Montenegro: 55.5% against a 55% threshold

sources.t: List of states with limited recognition

zones.name: Taking over an existing state or town
zones.who_owns: The existing state or municipality. The route tries to capture its government through force, votes or settlement.

rules.cite: South African Civil Aviation Offences Act
rules.says: After the Seychelles attempt, South Africa charged the mercenaries over the hijacking of an Air India aircraft and not over the coup attempt.
The state attorney general argued Rajneeshpuram's incorporation merged church and city. Federal and state courts later reached different results.
South Africa stripped black South Africans of citizenship and declared them citizens of the homelands.

zones.hook: Foreign governments, police and informers stop armed plots early. Towns remain under state and national law, so voters and courts there can only change what local government controls.
zones.can_you_build: Legally, move in and vote, as in Grafton, Marinaleda and New Hampshire. That wins local offices and leaves sovereignty where it was. Armed takeover is a crime in the places involved and most verified attempts failed.
facts: Comoros: Denard came with 43 men in 1978 and led a 500-strong guard for 11 years
Seychelles: 53 mercenaries, $300,000 raised against $5m advised
Rajneeshpuram: about 7,000 people on a $5.75m ranch
Free State Project: 20,000 pledges by 2016; about 6,232 movers by May 2022

sources.t: How to Start Your Own Country

zones.name: Indigenous and prior sovereignty
zones.who_owns: Disputed. The peoples concerned assert authority that predates the state, while the state usually treats it as a domestic matter.

rules.says: Land reserved for the Muscogee Nation in the 19th century was never disestablished and remains Indian country under the Major Crimes Act.
State courts share jurisdiction over crimes in Indian country by non-Indians against Indian victims.

rules.cite: Nunavut Act and Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act, 1993
rules.says: Created a territory for Inuit self-government within Canada.

zones.hook: States decide whether to accept the passports, recognise the government or pass the law. Courts rule on what the state's own laws mean, and a later case can narrow an earlier win.
zones.can_you_build: This route is open only to a people with an existing claim. The results found here came from negotiated land claims, court rulings and long use of a document, and each result stays within the existing state.
facts: Nunavut: 2,093,190 km², 36,858 people in 2021, agreement ratified by nearly 85%
Haudenosaunee passport issued since at least 1923
Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi reported 21,000 members in 1997

zones.name: Governments in exile and landless authority
zones.who_owns: Someone else holds the land. The exile body holds a claim, a community and whatever standing others give it.

rules.cite: Charter of the Tibetans in Exile, 1991, amended 2011
rules.says: Sets out the exile government's structure, with executive power in an elected Sikyong.

rules.cite: Constitutive and declarative theories of recognition
rules.says: One view says a state exists only when others recognise it. The other says recognition is not required if the Montevideo criteria are met.

zones.hook: The state in control simply keeps the territory. The host state decides how much activity it allows, and other governments decide whether to deal with the exile body.
zones.can_you_build: Keep a body running abroad with elections, members and funding from the diaspora. The Tibetan and Belarusian cases show this can last for decades without gaining any territory.
facts: Rada BNR in exile since 1919, described as the oldest existing government in exile as of 2026
Tibetan administration re-established 29 April 1959, recognised as sovereign by no country
Sahrawi refugee camps: 173,600 people (2023 estimate)

sources.t: Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic
List of states with limited recognition

cases.name: Territory sold between states
cases.founder: Governments of buying and selling states
cases.recognition: Each sale was a treaty between the parties
cases.cost: From about $4 per km² (Alaska) to $62,500 per km² (Danish West Indies), at the prices of the time
cases.story: States have bought land from each other for centuries, and a Wikipedia list records the deals where money was paid for sovereignty. Scotland paid Norway 4,000 marks sterling for the Isle of Man and the Hebrides in 1266. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about $7 per square kilometre. It paid Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about $4 per square kilometre, and paid Denmark $25 million for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies in 1916, which works out to $62,500 per square kilometre. Brazil paid Bolivia £2 million for Acre in 1903. The last entry on the list is Gwadar, which Pakistan bought from Muscat and Oman for £3 million in 1958. Every buyer and seller on the list is a state or a ruler. The list excludes leases and payments assigned to other purposes such as war damages. As part of the 1916 Danish deal, the United States also recognised Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland, a promise that came up again in the later offers to buy it.
cases.mechanism: Sovereignty can be sold by treaty, and the listed sales were all made between states or rulers.

sources.t: List of territory purchased by a sovereign nation from another sovereign nation
Proposed United States acquisition of Greenland

cases.name: US offers to buy Greenland
cases.founder: US governments, most recently President Donald Trump
cases.challenge: Danish and Greenlandic governments rejected each offer
cases.recognition: None sought; Denmark holds sovereignty
cases.story: The United States has discussed getting Greenland from Denmark since the 1860s. Secretary of State William Seward backed a purchase in 1867, and there were talks again in 1910. In 1946 the United States secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold bullion, which Denmark rejected. In 2019 President Trump said he wanted to buy the island, and Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen called the idea absurd, saying Greenland was not for sale. In his second term from 2025 Trump pressed again and spoke of tariffs against Denmark, and in January 2026 Greenland's leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said "We choose Denmark". Wikipedia's account says 85% of Greenlanders oppose an American takeover. Under Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum. On 22 September 2026 the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement that increases US involvement in Greenland's defence. No sale has taken place.
cases.mechanism: The United States could not buy territory without the seller's consent, and here the local people hold the decision on independence.

sources.t: Proposed United States acquisition of Greenland

cases.name: Romanov Empire (Anton Bakov)
cases.recognition: None found
cases.story: Anton Bakov is a Russian businessman and former State Duma member who says he restored the Russian Empire through a micronation founded in 2011. A micronation is a self-declared country that no state accepts. In 2014 it issued a manifesto naming the German prince Karl Emich of Leiningen as Emperor Nicholas III, and in 2017 it took the name Romanov Empire. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about US$31, and claimed about 4,000 by 2014. Bakov has held talks with several countries about buying land for it. As of 2017, talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. Nicholas III also wrote to Vladimir Putin asking for land in Yekaterinburg for a capital, and that request was denied. In July 2013 Bakov said his state had granted citizenship to Edward Snowden, then in Sheremetyevo Airport. In 2020 Bakov said a successor project called Arca Noë would be based in neutral Mediterranean waters near Venice, as a seastead.
cases.mechanism: A private buyer needs a government willing to give up sovereignty, and the governments approached did not agree.

cases.name: Guantanamo Bay lease
cases.laws: US military and federal law, tested in Boumediene v. Bush
cases.challenge: Cuba has protested since 1959; the base remains
cases.recognition: Lease between two states, disputed by Cuba
cases.story: The US Navy has held 117 square kilometres of land and water at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, since 1903, first as a coaling station. It is the oldest American naval base overseas. The rent was $2,000 a year in gold until 1934, when the United States changed it on its own to dollars, and since 1974 it has been $4,085 a year. The lease can only end by agreement of both sides or a full US military withdrawal. Since taking power in 1959, the Cuban government has protested that the base was imposed by force and is illegal under international law. Cuba has cashed only one rent cheque since the revolution, and Fidel Castro said that one was deposited by mistake in 1959. Since 2002 the base has held a detention camp for people captured in the war on terror. In Boumediene v. Bush in 2008, the US Supreme Court ruled that detainees there have a constitutional right to challenge their detention in court.
cases.mechanism: A lease with no end date lets one state run land another state still owns, even when the owner objects.

cases.name: New Territories lease
cases.stopped_by: The lease expired; the 1984 Joint Declaration arranged the handover
cases.recognition: Treaty between two states
cases.story: On 9 June 1898 Britain and Qing China signed the Second Convention of Peking, which leased the New Territories and New Kowloon, including 235 islands, to Britain for 99 years at no charge. Britain already held Hong Kong Island, ceded in 1842, and the Kowloon Peninsula, ceded in 1860. The lease came in a period when foreign powers forced similar deals on China; Germany had taken a 99-year lease on Kiautschou Bay a few months earlier. The source describes the Convention as a lease and an unequal treaty, and the Kowloon Walled City was left out of it. The lease was due to end on 30 June 1997. Under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration, Britain and the People's Republic of China agreed that all of it, including the ceded parts, would pass to China on 1 July 1997, and it did on schedule.
cases.mechanism: A lease has an end date that a state can enforce, and here that date ended British rule over the whole colony.

sources.t: Convention for the Extension of Hong Kong Territory

cases.name: Panama Canal Zone
cases.recognition: Concession under treaty
cases.story: The Canal Zone was a strip of 1,432 square kilometres across Panama, run by the United States from 1903 to 1979. It covered the canal and land about five miles either side of the centre line, leaving out Panama City and Colón. The Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty of 18 November 1903 allowed the United States to build the canal. A 1904 convention gave it use, occupation and control of the zone in perpetuity, which means with no end date. The zone had its capital at Balboa, a governor, and US dollars as currency, and the United States bought the land from its private and public owners. The first governors were military and from 1914 they were civilian. Despite the wording "in perpetuity", the zone was abolished on 1 October 1979 under the Torrijos–Carter Treaties signed two years earlier, and the area returned to Panama.
cases.mechanism: A treaty granting control forever can still be ended by a later treaty between the same states.

cases.name: Julian Assange at Ecuador's embassy
cases.stopped_by: Ecuador ended his asylum and invited British police in
cases.challenge: UK police guard; he stayed nearly seven years until Ecuador withdrew protection
cases.recognition: Asylum granted by Ecuador; not recognised by the UK
cases.story: On 19 June 2012 the WikiLeaks co-founder Julian Assange walked into Ecuador's embassy in London, a suite of rooms on the ground floor of a block of flats on Hans Crescent, and claimed diplomatic asylum. He was wanted by Swedish authorities for questioning over four alleged sexual offences and had breached bail. Ecuador granted asylum on 16 August 2012. Britain suggested it could use the Diplomatic and Consular Premises Act 1987 to enter and arrest him, then withdrew the suggestion after Ecuador's foreign minister called this a breach of international law and the Vienna Convention. Policing the embassy for the first two years reportedly cost £6.5 million. Swedish prosecutors dropped their investigation in May 2017. In April 2019 Ecuador's president Lenín Moreno accused Assange of repeatedly violating the terms of his asylum, and on 11 April 2019 British police, invited in by the Ecuadorian government, arrested him inside the embassy.
cases.mechanism: Local police generally stay out of an embassy unless the sending state invites them in, so the refuge lasts only as long as that state agrees.

cases.name: Fort St Angelo
cases.founder: Malta and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta
cases.recognition: Treaty with Malta
cases.story: Fort St Angelo stands in Birgu on Malta's Grand Harbour. The knights of the Order held it before moving their administrative centre to Valletta, and the British garrisoned it from 1800 to 1979. On 5 December 1998 Malta and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta signed a treaty giving the Order the upper part of the fort, including the Grand Master's House and the Chapel of St Anne, with limited extraterritoriality. That means Malta's normal authority is partly held back there. The treaty was ratified on 1 November 2001. It runs for 99 years, but the Maltese government can end it at any time after 50 years. Malta's flag must fly with the Order's flag in a prominent position. The Government of Malta remains the owner of the fort. Wikipedia's list of states with limited recognition treats the Order as a sovereign entity that claims neither statehood nor territory, with diplomatic relations with 114 UN members.
cases.mechanism: A state can grant limited special status to a recognised body by treaty and keep the right to take it back.

sources.t: List of states with limited recognition

cases.name: Mehran Karimi Nasseri at Charles de Gaulle
cases.passports: Lacked valid papers; refused those offered
cases.recognition: None sought
cases.story: Mehran Karimi Nasseri was an Iranian refugee who lived in the departure lounge of Terminal 1 at Charles de Gaulle Airport from 26 August 1988 until July 2006. He said his papers were stolen on the way to Britain; other accounts say he mailed them away himself. Britain sent him back to France when he had no passport, and at the French airport he could not prove his identity or status. His claim that Iran expelled him in 1977 has been disputed by later investigation. Belgium and France both offered him residency, but he refused to sign the papers because they listed him as Iranian and did not use his chosen name, "Sir, Alfred Mehran". He was hospitalised in 2006 and lived in Paris shelters for 16 years. He returned to the airport in September 2022 and died there two months later. His story inspired the 2004 film The Terminal. Airport international zones remain under the law of the country where they sit.
cases.mechanism: An airport transit area is under the host country's law, and living there produces no separate legal status.

cases.name: Edward Snowden at Sheremetyevo
cases.recognition: Asylum and later citizenship from Russia
cases.story: On 23 June 2013 Edward Snowden, who had leaked secret US surveillance documents, landed at Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow from Hong Kong. The United States had charged him under the Espionage Act of 1917 and for theft of government property, and the State Department revoked his passport. He had a seat reserved on an onward flight to Cuba and did not board it. WikiLeaks said he was on his way to asylum in Ecuador, and he held an Ecuadorian emergency travel document. The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that Cuba had told Moscow not to let him fly; the Washington Post contrasted this with other accounts. President Putin said Snowden was in the transit area, had committed no crime in Russia and was free to leave. Snowden stayed in the airport for about a month before Russia granted him asylum, and he became a naturalised Russian citizen in 2022.
cases.mechanism: A transit zone gave no independence from any state: Snowden left it only when Russia, the host state, granted asylum.

cases.name: UN headquarters zones
cases.recognition: Agreed with host states
cases.story: The United Nations' headquarters in New York and its offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi are run by the UN as international concessions, yet they remain subject to most local and national laws. A concession is an area where a state gives another body some authority. Because member states' delegates must be able to attend meetings in New York, the United States has a special visa category, the C-2, which lets otherwise barred foreign officials enter provided they stay near the headquarters. A similar arrangement between states is the Tomb of Suleyman Shah in Syria, set up as a Turkish concession by the 1921 Treaty of Ankara. The tomb was moved in 1973 because its site was to be flooded by a reservoir, and Turkey moved it again on its own in 2015. Syria called that move incompatible with the treaty, and Turkey plans to move the tomb back.
cases.mechanism: An international body can run premises inside a state, but most of that state's law still applies.

cases.name: Tangier International Zone
cases.stopped_by: Protecting powers agreed to abolish it; Moroccan sovereignty restored
cases.laws: International Legislative Assembly and Mixed Court
cases.recognition: Run by the signatory powers
cases.story: The Tangier International Zone covered 373 square kilometres around the Moroccan city of Tangier from 1923 to 1956. Several foreign powers ran it together. It had an appointed International Legislative Assembly, supervised by a Committee of Control made up of the consuls of Belgium, France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain. An Administrator held executive power. A Mixed Court of five judges, appointed by the Belgian, British, Spanish, French and Italian governments, replaced the separate consular courts that each power had run. The zone became known for tolerance and for its mixed culture and religions, and it drew writers and gay men from Western countries, many of whom could live openly there. In July 1952 the protecting powers met at Rabat and agreed to abolish the zone. Tangier rejoined the rest of Morocco when Morocco regained full sovereignty in 1956.
cases.mechanism: Foreign states can run a territory jointly by agreement, and it ends when they and the local sovereign decide to end it.

cases.name: Free City of Danzig
cases.laws: Own constitution and Volkstag under League oversight
cases.recognition: Created by treaty under League of Nations protection
cases.story: The Free City of Danzig, now Gdańsk in Poland, was set up on 15 November 1920 under Article 100 of the Treaty of Versailles. It was a city-state of the port and nearly 200 smaller places, 1,952 square kilometres with 366,730 people in 1923, mostly German. A League of Nations High Commissioner oversaw it. It had its own parliament, the Volkstag, and its own currency, the gulden, from 1923. Poland handled its foreign policy, defence, customs, railways and post under an imposed union, and had rights over port facilities. In 1921 Poland began building a rival port at Gdynia, whose trade passed Danzig's by 1933. The Nazi Party won 50% of the vote in the Volkstag election of 28 May 1933 and took over the Senate in June. Germany annexed the city on 1 September 1939, and Danzig police fought alongside German forces in the September Campaign. It was awarded to Poland on 1 August 1945.
cases.mechanism: A city-state guaranteed by an international body lasted only as long as the guarantors were willing and able to protect it.

cases.name: Free Territory of Trieste
cases.founder: UN Security Council and Treaty of Peace with Italy
cases.currency: Italian lira (Zone A); Triestine lira (Zone B)
cases.recognition: Created by treaty and UN Security Council resolution
cases.story: The Free Territory of Trieste was meant to be a neutral independent country between Italy and Yugoslavia, under the direct responsibility of the UN Security Council. The aim was to ease rival claims over a port with a mixed population. It was created by a protocol of the Treaty of Peace with Italy on 10 February 1947 and came into existence on 15 September 1947. The governor required by UN Resolution 16 was never appointed, so it never worked as a real independent state, though its formal status was generally respected. It was split in two instead: Zone A, the city and coast, under Allied military rule, and Zone B under Yugoslav rule, with separate versions of the lira. On 5 October 1954 the United States, Britain, Italy and Yugoslavia signed the London Memorandum, which ended Allied rule in Zone A. Italy took Zone A and Yugoslavia kept Zone B. The Treaty of Osimo, signed in 1975 and ratified in 1977, settled the border.
cases.mechanism: A state created by the UN on paper never took shape because the governor it required was never appointed.

cases.name: Corpus separatum for Jerusalem
cases.stopped_by: Rejection by Arab leaders and the 1948 war
cases.recognition: Adopted by the UN General Assembly, never implemented
cases.story: Corpus separatum is Latin for "separated body". It was the plan to place Jerusalem and its surroundings under international government as part of the UN Partition Plan for Palestine, adopted by the UN General Assembly with a two-thirds majority in November 1947. The city was to have special status because of its importance to the Abrahamic religions. Its founding statute was to be reviewed after ten years and put to a referendum. The idea drew on the Vatican's long-held concern for the Christian holy places. The plan was never carried out. Palestinian and other Arab leaders rejected it first, then the 1948 Arab–Israeli War left Jerusalem split between Israel in the west and Jordan in the east. It came up again as a main issue at the Lausanne Conference of 1949. In 2012 the European Parliament and the UN General Assembly expressed support for Jerusalem as a dual capital of Israel and a State of Palestine, with exact positions varying.
cases.mechanism: A General Assembly plan for an international city does not take effect unless the parties on the ground accept it or someone enforces it.

cases.name: Condominiums: New Hebrides, Andorra, Brčko
cases.recognition: Set by agreement between the states concerned
cases.story: A condominium is territory shared by two or more powers. New Hebrides was a French–British condominium from 1906 until it became independent in 1980 as the republic now called Vanuatu. Nauru was run jointly by Australia, New Zealand and Britain until independence in 1968. Brčko District in Bosnia and Herzegovina, created on 8 March 2000, is held jointly by the country's two internal entities because of its mixed population; it covers 493 square kilometres with 83,516 people. Andorra was once treated in French law as a French–Spanish condominium, though it is now more commonly classed as a co-principality because it is a sovereign state. Its head of state is shared by two foreigners by virtue of their offices: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain. These arrangements come from agreements between the states involved, and the cases of New Hebrides, Nauru and Andorra show that a shared territory can end up independent.
cases.mechanism: Shared rule by agreement can last for decades and can lead to independence, as it did for Vanuatu and Nauru.

cases.name: Cyprus Buffer Zone and Pyla
cases.laws: Patrolled by the UN force in Cyprus
cases.recognition: UN-administered ceasefire line
cases.story: The UN Buffer Zone in Cyprus, also called the Green Line, runs 180 kilometres across the island and covers 346 square kilometres. It began in 1964 and was extended after the ceasefire of 16 August 1974, which followed the Turkish invasion and the island's partition into the Republic of Cyprus and the largely unrecognised Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. UN peacekeepers patrol it. It ranges from under 20 metres to over 7 kilometres wide and cuts through the centre of Nicosia. Despite this, some 10,000 people live and farm in villages inside the zone, including Deneia, Athienou and Troulloi. Pyla is known as one of the few villages left in Cyprus where Greek and Turkish Cypriots still live side by side. Crossings were very limited until April 2003, when the Turkish Cypriot administration eased restrictions after nearly 30 years. No attempt to declare a separate state in the zone appeared in the source.
cases.mechanism: A peacekeeping strip does not end the claims of the states on either side, so people inside it stay part of an existing state.

sources.t: United Nations Buffer Zone in Cyprus

cases.name: Korean DMZ villages
cases.recognition: Armistice arrangement
cases.story: The Korean Demilitarized Zone was created by the armistice of 27 July 1953, when each side moved its troops back 2,000 metres from the front. It is about 250 kilometres long and 4 kilometres wide, and its edges are among the most heavily armed borders in the world. Only two settlements are allowed to stay inside it. Daeseong-dong, also called Tae Sung Dong or Freedom Village, is on the southern side and is governed and protected by the UN Command. Its residents, 218 people in 2008, descend from those who owned the land before the war. They must generally spend at least 240 nights a year there to keep their residency. They count as South Korean citizens but do not pay tax or do military service. Kijŏng-dong, or Peace Village, is on the northern side, with brightly painted concrete buildings. Access is granted only by North Korea or the UN Command, and the armistice committee allowed only these two villages to remain.
cases.mechanism: Living inside an armistice zone depends on permission from the armistice bodies, and residents keep the citizenship of a state on one side.

cases.name: Chernobyl self-settlers
cases.recognition: None sought
cases.story: The samosely, meaning self-settlers, live inside the 30-kilometre Chernobyl Exclusion Zone in Ukraine and Belarus without official approval. Some refused to leave after the 1986 disaster and others slipped back after the area was cordoned off. About 1,200 people returned in 1986, out of about 100,000 evacuated. Most were elderly people who had lived there before the disaster, though some were outsiders disaffected with life elsewhere. Many had been told they could go home in a few days and faced discrimination in resettlement areas. An official census counted 314 in 2007 and there were 135 by 2017. They mainly live in the town of Chernobyl and 11 other villages. Over 25 years there were more than 900 deaths and one known birth, a girl born on 25 August 1999. The decline comes mainly from old age. Nobody among them has declared a state. They remain residents of the countries that administer the zone.
cases.mechanism: Evacuation orders can go unenforced in practice, yet people staying there gain no separate legal standing.

cases.name: The record of independence referendums
cases.recognition: Varies by case
cases.story: An independence referendum lets residents vote on whether their territory should become a sovereign state. A Yes vote does not always bring independence. Wikipedia's table, as retrieved in November 2026, lists about 123 votes since Chile in 1817. By a count made for this map, 59 ended in a No, 31 in a Yes with independence and recognition, 16 in a Yes with no independence, and 12 in a Yes with control on the ground but no general recognition. The rest ended in associated status, a contested independence, or continuing negotiation. Western Australia voted Yes in 1933 and stayed in Australia. Nevis voted Yes in 1998 and fell short of the two-thirds majority required. Quebec voted No in 1980 and 1995. Iraqi Kurdistan voted Yes in 2005 and 2017 without result. Votes held under terms agreed with the parent state can be binding and accepted abroad. Votes held without its consent can lead to unilateral declarations and partly recognised states.
cases.mechanism: A referendum carries real weight when its terms were agreed with the parent state; a Yes without that agreement rarely brings recognition.

cases.name: South Sudan
cases.founder: Sudan People's Liberation Army/Movement and the Khartoum government, under the 2005 agreement
cases.recognition: Independent state, with the result recognised
cases.story: South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after a vote held from 9 to 15 January that year. The referendum came from the 2005 Naivasha Agreement between the central government in Khartoum and the Sudan People's Liberation Army/Movement, which set the terms and the date in advance. Preparing it needed a census, delayed three times, and voter registration, with unmapped minefields in the south, up to 5 million nomadic Sudanese, and up to 2 million displaced southerners in camps around Khartoum. The final results, published on 7 February 2011, showed 98.83% for secession on a turnout of 97.58%. Ballots were suspended in 10 of 79 counties for exceeding 100% turnout, but the result stood well over the required 60% turnout. A parallel vote for Abyei on joining the south was postponed over disputes about borders and who could vote, and it was later postponed indefinitely.
cases.mechanism: A secession agreed in a peace deal with the parent state, with a date fixed in advance, led to accepted independence.

cases.name: Eritrea
cases.recognition: Independent state, with the result recognised
cases.story: Eritrea was an Italian colony from 1890 and came under British administration after the Second World War. In 1950 the UN voted to combine it with Ethiopia in a federation with some autonomy. By 1962 Emperor Haile Selassie had ended that autonomy and made Eritrea a province. An armed rebellion followed, and the Eritrean War of Independence ended in May 1991, when the Eritrean People's Liberation Front defeated Ethiopian forces. The Front had first proposed a referendum in 1981. Transitional governments planned the process, and a UN mission known as UNOVER, set up by General Assembly Resolution 47/114 in December 1992, observed and verified it. Voting ran from 23 to 25 April 1993. The result was 99.83% Yes: 1,100,260 votes against 1,822. Independence was declared on 27 April 1993. The source's text gives turnout above 98% while its results table gives 93.93%.
cases.mechanism: Military victory followed by a UN-verified vote produced a recognised state.

cases.name: Timor-Leste
cases.founder: Timorese independence movement, with UN organisation
cases.recognition: Independent state from 20 May 2002
cases.story: Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975, soon after Fretilin declared independence, and annexed it the following year. The UN did not recognise the annexation. On 27 January 1999 Indonesian president B. J. Habibie asked the UN to hold a vote giving a choice between greater autonomy and independence. On 30 August 1999, under a UN mission, 78.5% of voters rejected special autonomy within Indonesia, on a turnout of 98.93%. Mass violence and destruction of infrastructure followed. On 15 September the UN Security Council approved a multinational force, INTERFET, to restore order. Indonesia's assembly repealed its 1978 annexation resolution, and the UN Transitional Administration in East Timor, UNTAET, governed the territory until it achieved recognised independence on 20 May 2002. Many Indonesians, including the government, call the vote a consultation and not a referendum.
cases.mechanism: An occupation the UN never accepted ended when the occupying state agreed to a vote and the UN then ran the territory until independence.

cases.name: Montenegro
cases.founder: Government of Montenegro, under a constitutional right
cases.laws: Article 60, Constitutional Charter of Serbia and Montenegro
cases.recognition: Independent state; result accepted by all five Security Council permanent members
cases.story: Montenegro left its union with Serbia by using a right written into the union's own constitution. Article 60 of the 2003 Constitutional Charter required at least three years to pass before a member state could leave, and it required a referendum. The government wanted a simple majority. The opposition insisted on a threshold, and a controversial rule of 55% was adopted. On 21 May 2006 Yes won 55.5% with a turnout of 86.49%: 230,711 votes against 184,954, narrowly clearing the bar. All five permanent members of the UN Security Council recognised the preliminary result by 23 May. Parliament formally declared independence on 3 June, which dissolved Serbia and Montenegro. Serbia declared itself the legal successor of the union. The United States, China, Russia and the European Union said they would respect the result. An earlier vote in 1992 had gone against independence.
cases.mechanism: A union's constitution with an exit clause gave a clear legal path, and outside powers accepted the result within days.

cases.name: Kosovo
cases.founder: Assembly of Kosovo; Prime Minister Hashim Thaçi and President Fatmir Sejdiu
cases.laws: UN Resolution 1244 administration, then own institutions
cases.challenge: Serbia took it to the International Court of Justice; the court found no violation
cases.recognition: 110 UN members, Taiwan, Cook Islands, Niue; 8 withdrew; not a UN member
cases.story: Kosovo was an autonomous province within Serbia in Yugoslavia. In 1990 its assembly voted to declare independence, and only Albania recognised that declaration. After the Kosovo War, UN Security Council Resolution 1244 placed it under the UN Mission in Kosovo from 1999, with a NATO-led force providing security. Before and during the handover, an estimated 100,000 Serbs and other non-Albanians fled. On 17 February 2008, 109 of 120 assembly members adopted a new declaration of independence. Serbia called it illegal and in 2008 persuaded the UN General Assembly, by 77 votes to 6 with 74 abstentions, to ask the International Court of Justice for an opinion. On 22 July 2010 the court ruled 10 to 4 that the declaration did not violate international law. Talks led to a 2013 Brussels deal between Belgrade and Pristina. Kosovo is recognised by 110 UN members, Taiwan, the Cook Islands and Niue, and 8 other UN members withdrew recognition. It belongs to the IMF and the World Bank.
cases.mechanism: The court said declaring independence does not itself break international law, but membership of the UN still depends on other states.

sources.t: List of states with limited recognition

cases.name: Bougainville
cases.recognition: Not independent; the result is accepted as a vote, and the status awaits Papua New Guinea's parliament
cases.story: Bougainville is an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea. Independence was discussed as early as 1968, and it was made a province in 1976 after Papua New Guinea became independent. A civil war from 1988 to 1998 ended with a 2001 agreement that promised a referendum. The vote ran from 23 November to 7 December 2019 and asked voters to choose greater autonomy or independence. Independence won 176,928 votes to 3,043, or 98.31%, with turnout of 87.38%. The vote was non-binding, and the national parliament has the final decision. In July 2021 the two governments agreed that Bougainville would become independent by 2027, pending ratification by Papua New Guinea's parliament. In July 2026 the Bougainville Independence Leaders Consultation Forum recommended 1 September 2030 as the target date. Parliament had still not ratified the agreement at that point.
cases.mechanism: A peace agreement can promise a vote without promising the outcome, leaving the final decision with the parent state's parliament.

cases.name: New Caledonia and Kanaky
cases.founder: Kanak independence parties and the French state, under the Nouméa Accord
cases.recognition: French territory; independence rejected in three votes, the last boycotted
cases.story: New Caledonia is a French territory in the South Pacific. The Matignon Agreements of 1988 and the Nouméa Accord of 1998, signed by France and the main parties on both sides, set a 20-year transition and allowed up to three votes. Voters rejected independence by 57% in 2018 and 53% in 2020. The third vote on 12 December 2021 took place despite a Kanak boycott. Their leaders had asked for delay after a COVID-19 outbreak that caused 280 deaths, saying Kanak mourning rituals could last a year. Opponents replied that the outbreak had declined by mid-November and accused them of using it as an excuse. The No side took 96.5% on a turnout of 43.87%. President Macron suggested changes including unfreezing voter rolls, which would make more French nationals eligible to vote. After the 2024 unrest, New Zealand's foreign minister questioned the vote's legitimacy, and France's ambassador to the Pacific criticised his remarks.
cases.mechanism: An agreed series of votes can run its full course and still leave the question open when one side boycotts the last one.

cases.name: Catalonia 2017
cases.founder: Government and Parliament of Catalonia; President Carles Puigdemont
cases.recognition: None; result not recognised
cases.story: The Catalan parliament approved a referendum law on 6 September 2017, with 52 opposing members boycotting. Spain's Constitutional Court suspended the law on 7 September at the request of the Spanish government, which called it a breach of the constitution. The vote went ahead on 1 October, with National Police and Civil Guard force at polling stations. Yes took 2,044,038 votes, or 90.18%, on a turnout of 43.03%. The Catalan government estimated that up to 770,000 votes could not be cast because of the police crackdown. Observers it had invited said the vote fell short of international standards. The court declared the law void on 17 October. On 27 October the Catalan parliament declared independence. The same day Spain's Senate voted 214 to 47 to invoke Article 155 of the constitution and take direct control of some Catalan powers. In the 2024 Catalan elections independence parties lost control of the government, and an amnesty was declared that year for crimes linked to the referendum.
cases.mechanism: A region's vote held against a constitutional court's order gave it no legal effect, and the parent state took direct control.

cases.name: Scotland 2014
cases.founder: Scottish Government; First Minister Alex Salmond
cases.recognition: Result accepted by both governments
cases.story: Scotland's 2014 vote is an example of a referendum agreed with the parent state. The Scottish Government and the UK government negotiated until October 2012, when they reached the Edinburgh Agreement. Voters were asked "Should Scotland be an independent country?" on 18 September 2014. The voting age was lowered for the occasion. The main campaigns were Yes Scotland and Better Together. No won with 2,001,926 votes, or 55.3%, against 1,617,989, or 44.7%. Turnout of 84.6% was the highest for any UK election or referendum since January 1910. The Scottish National Party has said there should be a repeat vote now that the United Kingdom has left the European Union. Scotland remains part of the United Kingdom.
cases.mechanism: With the parent state's agreement a vote is legally clean, and independence then depends on winning it.

cases.name: Republic of Biafra
cases.recognition: Gabon, Haiti, Côte d'Ivoire, Tanzania, Zambia
cases.story: Biafra declared independence from Nigeria on 30 May 1967. Its territory was Nigeria's former Eastern Region, mainly Igbo with sizeable Ijaw, Efik, Ibibio and other populations, and it had about 13.5 million people. The declaration came from Eastern Region governor Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, after ethnic tensions, military coups and a 1966 anti-Igbo pogrom. Nigeria's military moved to retake the territory, starting the Nigerian Civil War. Five states recognised Biafra officially: Gabon, Haiti, Côte d'Ivoire, Tanzania and Zambia. France, Portugal, Israel, South Africa and Rhodesia gave de facto recognition and covert military support. Biafra issued its own pound. After nearly three years of war, in which Wikipedia reports around two million Biafran civilians died, Ojukwu fled to Côte d'Ivoire. Philip Effiong oversaw the surrender, and the territory rejoined Nigeria on 15 January 1970. Igbo nationalism has grown more militant since the 1990s.
cases.mechanism: Recognition by five states did not save a breakaway state that lost the war against its parent.

cases.name: Abkhazia
cases.recognition: Russia, Syria, Nicaragua, Venezuela, South Ossetia, Transnistria; three others withdrew
cases.story: Abkhazia declared independence from Georgia in 1999, and Georgia still claims it as sovereign territory. It is recognised by four UN members, Russia, Syria, Nicaragua and Venezuela, and by two other unrecognised states, South Ossetia and Transnistria. Three more UN members, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Nauru, recognised it and later withdrew. Abkhazia keeps informal missions abroad and is not a UN member. Two theories of statehood apply. The declarative theory, from the 1933 Montevideo Convention, asks for territory, population, government and the capacity to deal with other states, whether or not others recognise it. The constitutive theory says a state exists only once existing states recognise it.
cases.mechanism: Control on the ground and a few recognitions leave a territory outside the UN, and small states can withdraw recognition.

sources.t: List of states with limited recognition

cases.name: South Ossetia
cases.recognition: Russia, Syria, Nicaragua, Venezuela, Abkhazia, Transnistria; two others withdrew
cases.story: South Ossetia declared independence from Georgia in 1992, after a referendum that year, and held another vote in 2006. Both went for independence, and neither brought general recognition. Georgia claims it as sovereign territory. Four UN members recognise it, Russia, Syria, Nicaragua and Venezuela, along with Abkhazia and Transnistria. Tuvalu and Nauru recognised it and later withdrew. It is also one of the few recognisers of the Sahrawi Republic. Wikipedia's referendum table marks its result as de facto independence, unrecognised.
cases.mechanism: A repeated Yes vote held without the parent state's agreement did not widen recognition.

sources.t: List of states with limited recognition

cases.name: Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic
cases.pop: About 173,600 in refugee camps (2023); 40,000 in held areas (2010)
cases.currency: Sahrawi peseta de jure; dirham, dinar, ouguiya and euro in use
cases.challenge: Morocco holds most of the territory
cases.recognition: African Union member; recognition counts vary, 33 to 46 UN members
cases.story: Western Sahara was the Spanish colony of Spanish Sahara until 1975, when Spain gave it up and Morocco annexed most of it. On 27 February 1976 the Polisario Front proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic at Bir Lehlou. It claims 266,000 square kilometres and controls about 90,000, the easternmost fifth, under a 1991 ceasefire. Its official capital, Laayoune, is held by Morocco, so its provisional capital was moved to Tifariti in 2008, and daily government runs from the Rabuni refugee camp in Tindouf, Algeria, where about 173,600 people lived in 2023. It is a full member of the African Union. Counts of recognition differ by source: one Wikipedia page says 46 UN members and another 33, and 38 others have withdrawn or suspended recognition pending a referendum. Nine UN members officially recognise Morocco's annexation. The UN lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory, and General Assembly Resolution 34/37 recognised the people's right to self-determination.
cases.mechanism: Regional membership and dozens of recognitions have not given it control of most of the land it claims.

sources.t: List of states with limited recognition

cases.name: Republic of New Afrika
cases.founder: Supporters of Malcolm X; Robert F. Williams, first president
cases.stopped_by: Federal and state raids and arrests
cases.recognition: None
cases.story: The Republic of New Afrika is a Black nationalist organisation founded in 1968. It seeks an independent country in the Black Belt of the American South, reparations from the US government for slavery and Jim Crow, and a plebiscite of African Americans on citizenship. Its founding conference adopted a declaration, a constitution and a provisional government, and it claims Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina as "subjugated national territory". It announced a capital in Hinds County, Mississippi, on a member's farm. There were shootouts at New Bethel Baptist Church in 1969 and in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1971, in which law-enforcement officers were killed and injured. Members were prosecuted and said they acted in self-defence. The organisation declined in the early 1970s, which Wikipedia attributes mainly to government raids and mass arrests. Its member Chokwe Lumumba, its vice president from 1971, later became a lawyer and was mayor of Jackson from 2013 to 2014.
cases.mechanism: A provisional government claiming land by declaration, with no agreement from the state, met raids and prosecutions and took no territory.

cases.name: Palau, Micronesia and the Marshall Islands compacts
cases.founder: United States and the Freely Associated States
cases.recognition: Sovereign states in free association with the United States
cases.story: The Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau were part of the US-run Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, a UN arrangement meant to lead to self-government or independence. Each became a sovereign state in free association with the United States. Their compacts took effect on 3 November 1986 for Micronesia, 21 October 1986 for the Marshall Islands and 1 October 1994 for Palau, whose agreement was signed in 1986 and took eight more years to come into force. Referendums in 1983 and 1984 preceded this. Under the compacts, the United States pays guaranteed financial assistance and provides access to some US services, and in return it holds full authority over their defence. The agreements have no end date, though the economic terms are renewed periodically, most recently for 2024 to 2043 under US Public Law 118-42.
cases.mechanism: A territory can reach sovereignty by trading its defence authority to a larger state for funding, by treaty.

cases.name: Bob Denard in the Comoros
cases.recognition: Ruled through a recognised president of the Comoros
cases.story: Bob Denard was a French mercenary who made four attempts on the government of the Comoros between 1975 and 1995. On the orders of Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's Africa adviser, he removed president Ahmed Abdallah in 1975. On 13 May 1978 he returned with 43 men, with Rhodesian government support, and overthrew Ali Soilih, who was killed on 29 May; the official account, that he was shot while trying to escape, is not generally believed. Abdallah returned as president, and Denard ran his 500-strong presidential guard for 11 years, becoming a citizen and holding hotels and land. In 1989 Abdallah was shot in his office, allegedly by a military officer, and Denard agreed to leave after meeting French officials. On 27 September 1995 he landed with 33 men against president Djohar. The French army ended the attempt on 4 October, and he surrendered. A French court gave him a five-year suspended term in June 2006, and on appeal in July 2007 four years with three suspended, which he never served for health reasons. During the trial, witnesses said French intelligence had supported him.
cases.mechanism: A small armed force can capture a weak state's government but cannot keep it once the regional power withdraws support.

cases.name: Seychelles coup attempt, 1981
cases.founder: Mike Hoare, with South African government encouragement
cases.stopped_by: Airport security check and Seychelles forces
cases.story: On 25 November 1981 a group of 53 mercenaries led by Mike Hoare tried to overthrow Seychelles prime minister France-Albert René and restore former president James Mancham. Hoare advised raising $5 million but only $300,000 was found. The men arrived at Seychelles International Airport disguised as rugby players and members of a beer-drinking club, with weapons in their baggage. Airport staff found an AK-47 in one man's luggage and raised the alarm. After a long firefight in which one soldier and one mercenary died, most mercenaries hijacked an Air India aircraft to Durban. In South Africa they were charged with minor aviation offences and only eight of the 43 accused were charged. Hoare was sentenced to ten years and released in May 1985 under an amnesty. Seychelles sentenced four men captured there to death on 6 July 1982 and two others to prison. All six were pardoned after talks and a $3 million payment to René. UN and South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission inquiries condemned South Africa's role.
cases.mechanism: A plot against a recognised government failed at the first checkpoint, and the state behind it later faced international condemnation.

cases.name: Wonga Coup, Equatorial Guinea
cases.cost: $180,000 deposit paid for arms; about $285,000 from Thatcher
cases.story: In 2004 a group organised by mainly British financiers planned to replace Equatorial Guinea's president Teodoro Obiang with the exiled politician Severo Moto. Prosecutors alleged Moto was to give oil rights to companies tied to the plotters. On 7 March 2004 police at Harare airport in Zimbabwe impounded a Boeing 727 from South Africa with three crew and 64 former soldiers, and arrested former SAS officer Simon Mann by the runway as he waited for arms to be loaded. Mann said the weapons were for guarding diamond mines in Congo. On 9 March Nick du Toit and 14 others were arrested in Equatorial Guinea, and du Toit testified that he had been recruited by Mann to install Moto. The name comes from a letter Mann wrote from prison asking for "a large splodge of wonga". On 13 January 2005 Mark Thatcher pleaded guilty in South Africa to helping finance the plot, having sent about $285,000, and received a four-year suspended sentence and a fine of about $560,000.
cases.mechanism: A privately funded armed takeover collapsed at a foreign airport, and one backer was convicted under South Africa's anti-mercenary law.

cases.name: Operation Red Dog, Dominica
cases.founder: Mike Perdue, Wolfgang Droege, Don Black, Sydney Burnett-Alleyne
cases.stopped_by: US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms
cases.cost: About $70,000 collected for weapons and reconnaissance
cases.story: Operation Red Dog was a 1981 plot to overthrow the government of Dominica, led by Eugenia Charles, and restore former prime minister Patrick John. Participants included Ku Klux Klan member Mike Perdue, German-Canadian Nazi Wolfgang Droege and American white nationalist Don Black. Perdue had first aimed at Grenada and hoped to set up lucrative businesses. Perdue testified that he received $10,000 from a lawyer and used $70,000 from businessmen for weapons, dynamite and reconnaissance trips. In February 1981 the original boat captain and crew backed out. Perdue then approached captain Michael Howell, telling him the CIA needed his boat. Howell went to the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. John was arrested in Dominica on 25 April. On 27 April, Droege and eight other men were arrested in New Orleans as they prepared to board, with automatic weapons, dynamite and a Nazi flag. Three undercover agents were in the group. There were no casualties.
cases.mechanism: Plotters who need boats and guns must pass through other countries' laws, and one informant was enough to stop this plot.

cases.name: Rajneeshpuram and Antelope
cases.founder: Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh and Ma Anand Sheela
cases.stopped_by: Criminal prosecutions and the leader's plea deal
cases.challenge: A federal judge ruled against it in 1985; Oregon courts later upheld it as legal, after it was empty
cases.recognition: None sought
cases.story: In 1981 followers of the teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh bought the 64,281-acre Big Muddy Ranch in central Oregon for $5.75 million. Within three years they had built a city of up to 7,000 people with police, a fire service, an airstrip and a post office. Nearby Antelope had under 60 people. As more followers moved in, Antelope voted in April 1982 on dissolving itself to avoid takeover, and the followers had enough votes to defeat it. In May 1982 the ranch voted to incorporate as a city. Oregon's attorney general argued the city merged church and state, and 1000 Friends of Oregon argued it broke land-use law. In 1984 some leaders carried out a bioterror attack to depress turnout in county elections, sickening 751 people and hospitalising 45. A plot to kill a US attorney also followed. Rajneesh entered a plea on immigration charges and agreed to leave the country, and the commune disbanded in 1985. The ranch was sold in 1988 at a sheriff's auction for $4.5 million, and it is now a Young Life camp.
cases.mechanism: Moving voters into a small town can capture local government legally, and that gives no protection from state and federal criminal law.

cases.name: Free State Project
cases.recognition: None sought
cases.story: The Free State Project began in 2001 with an article by Jason Sorens titled "Let's Secede!", which proposed an independent libertarian nation or concessions from the US government. He soon backed away from secession, saying it was not part of the project's approach, although it still matters to many members. He calculated that 20,000 libertarians moving to one small state could change it. Members chose New Hampshire in 2003 and signed a pledge to move within five years of reaching 20,000 signatures. The count reached 20,000 on 3 February 2016. By May 2022 about 6,232 people had moved. In the 2017–2018 term, Free Staters held 17 of the 400 seats in the state House. Former executive director Carla Gericke formed a movement in 2026 called NH Exit Now, advocating secession. Its site claims 42% of voters favoured a ballot question in 2022, a figure that comes from the group itself. New Hampshire remains a US state.
cases.mechanism: Moving voters can win seats inside a state, and this does not change the state's place in the union.

cases.name: Free Town Project, Grafton
cases.recognition: None sought
cases.story: After the Free State Project chose New Hampshire, a splinter group formed in 2004 to move to the small town of Grafton and push for legal changes there. The town attracted them because it had no zoning laws and a very low property tax. It was also home to John Babiarz, a Libertarian Party figure who had twice run for governor. No records were kept of how many came, but the population rose from 1,138 in 2000 to 1,340 in 2010, with nearly all newcomers men. Participants lived in yurts, recreational vehicles, trailers, tents and shipping containers. The changes they voted through included a 30% cut in the town's already small budget and removing funding for the county's senior-citizens council. Lawsuits they filed to set legal precedents raised the town's costs. A book by Matt Hongoltz-Hetling linked the group to rising bear activity after attacks in the area, while the state's bear biologist said in 2023 that nothing suggested the bear population had spiked.
cases.mechanism: Settling a small town can change its budget by ordinary votes, and everything else stays under state and federal law.

cases.name: Marinaleda
cases.founder: Juan Manuel Sánchez Gordillo and the Workers' Unity Collective
cases.recognition: Ordinary municipality
cases.story: Marinaleda is a Spanish municipality of about 2,562 people in Seville province. The Workers' Unity Collective won 9 of 11 council seats in the first post-Franco elections in 1979, and Juan Manuel Sánchez Gordillo remained mayor until 2023. In 1980, 700 people held a 13-day hunger strike over pay. In 1984 residents occupied the Cordobilla marsh for 30 days to demand irrigation for El Humoso, a farm owned by the Duke of Infantado, and in 1991 a 1,200-hectare tract of that farm was handed over for local use. A cooperative founded in 1997 farms it, and a food plant followed three years later. Self-built housing costs no more than 15 euros a month. Critics say almost 66% of municipal income comes from higher government. The same source says it received about 6.61% less than the regional average in 2011. It remains a part of Spain, subject to Spanish law.
cases.mechanism: A town can reorganise land and housing through elected office and pressure on the state, while staying inside the state.

cases.name: Slab City
cases.recognition: None
cases.story: Slab City is an unincorporated, off-the-grid community in Imperial County, California, whose slogan is "The last free place". It takes its name from the concrete slabs left when the Marines dismantled Camp Dunlap, a 631-acre training base commissioned in 1942. All buildings were gone by 1956. In 1961 the Department of Defense passed the land to California by a quitclaim deed, which means transfer without conditions. Drifters and then owners of recreational vehicles came for free camping. The Washington Post reported in 2020 that the population might reach 4,000 in winter and fall to about 150 in summer. Reports conflict on who owns the land, some saying the state of California and others from 1993 saying a building contractor. As of 2021 California had not decided to sell, and its Lands Commission was considering an appraisal and cleanup of military waste. In 2015 residents formed a community group to try to prevent a sale.
cases.mechanism: Lack of enforcement can leave people living freely on public land, and the owner can change that at any time.

cases.name: Kingdom of Lovely
cases.recognition: None
cases.story: The Kingdom of Lovely came from How to Start Your Own Country, a six-part British comedy documentary shown in August and September 2005. The presenter, comedian Danny Wallace, claimed his flat in Bow, east London, as territory, proclaimed himself king and sent a declaration of independence to the Prime Minister. The project was partly internet-based. At its peak 58,165 people registered as citizens on its website, citizensrequired.com, which is no longer active. A final gathering of citizens took place in Leicester Square, where Wallace revealed the name. Wikipedia dates the claim from 1 January 2005 to 19 May 2013. No state recognised it.
cases.mechanism: Declaring independence in a flat has no legal effect, since the building stays under the state.

sources.t: How to Start Your Own Country

cases.name: Bantustans: Transkei, Bophuthatswana, Venda, Ciskei
cases.stopped_by: End of apartheid; Interim Constitution of 1994
cases.laws: Homeland constitutions under South African acts
cases.recognition: South Africa only; no other government
cases.story: Bantustans, or homelands, were territories set aside for black South Africans under apartheid. The Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set out a plan for them to become self-governing and eventually nominally independent. The Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 stripped black South Africans of South African citizenship and declared them citizens of these homelands. South Africa declared four of them independent: Transkei in 1976, Bophuthatswana in 1977, Venda in 1979 and Ciskei in 1981. Ciskei held a referendum in 1980 that Wikipedia marks as recognised by South Africa alone. Anti-apartheid forces and every other government refused to recognise these declarations. Transkei served as a testing ground for the policy. An Interim Constitution effectively abolished the Bantustans with the end of apartheid in 1994, and Bophuthatswana's leader Lucas Mangope later led a party that contested that termination.
cases.mechanism: Independence granted by a parent state to serve its own policy failed the recognition test, since no other state accepted it.

cases.name: Haudenosaunee passport
cases.challenge: Refused by the UK in 2010 and by Canada at the border
cases.recognition: Accepted case by case by Japan, Israel and Ireland; rejected by the EU
cases.story: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, also called the Iroquois, has issued its own passports since at least 1923, when one went to Cayuga statesman Deskaheh to travel to the League of Nations in Geneva. The modern form has been used since 1977. Acceptance is uneven. Japan admitted a delegation on it in 2005. In July 2010 Britain refused it for the lacrosse team travelling to the World Championship, and the United States offered the players US passports, which they rejected. Israel accepted the team's passports in July 2018, subject to Canadian assurances about re-entry, and Ireland accepted them in August 2022. The European Union and the Isle of Man list it as a "fantasy passport", the US, UK and Canadian governments have refused to endorse it, and it is not accepted for entry into Canada. In early 2010 a Kahnawake delegation was stranded in El Salvador for weeks trying to return on it.
cases.mechanism: A nation's own passport works only where other states choose to honour it, and acceptance has been decided case by case.

cases.name: McGirt v. Oklahoma
cases.laws: Tribal and federal jurisdiction under the Major Crimes Act
cases.challenge: Narrowed by Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta in 2022
cases.recognition: US Supreme Court ruling
cases.story: In McGirt v. Oklahoma, decided in 2020, the US Supreme Court held that the land Congress reserved for the Muscogee Nation in the 19th century was never officially ended and remains Indian country under the Major Crimes Act. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote for the five-member majority. That meant Oklahoma could not prosecute Native Americans for crimes committed there. Oklahoma's Court of Criminal Appeals then applied the same reasoning to nine other Indigenous nations, so almost all of eastern Oklahoma counts as Indian country. Those cases go to tribal and federal courts. Courts first vacated past convictions, but less than a year later the state appeals court ruled McGirt was not retroactive. In 2022, in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, the Supreme Court held that state courts share jurisdiction over crimes by non-Indians against Indian victims in Indian country. The ruling changed who may prosecute crimes on this land and did not make the nations independent states.
cases.mechanism: A reservation set up by Congress continues until it is disestablished, though later rulings can narrow what follows from that.

cases.name: Nunavut
cases.founder: Inuit organisations and the government of Canada
cases.recognition: Canadian territory
cases.story: Nunavut is Canada's largest territory, created through a land-claims negotiation. In 1976 the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and the federal government began discussing a division of the Northwest Territories. The land-claims agreement was completed in September 1992 and ratified by nearly 85% of voters in a referendum. On 9 July 1993 Parliament passed the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act and the Nunavut Act, and the new territory began on 1 April 1999 with Iqaluit as its capital. It covers 2,093,190 square kilometres, with 36,858 people in 2021, most of them Inuit, and an estimated 43,091 in the third quarter of 2026. The Act provided the territory to the Inuit for self-government. A premier chosen by the assembly leads it, and a council of elders advises on using Inuit knowledge in government. It is a territory of Canada, with no claim to be a state.
cases.mechanism: A people can obtain a territory and self-government through negotiated law, staying inside the state.

cases.name: Hawaiian sovereignty movement
cases.founder: Native Hawaiian groups including Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi and the Nation of Hawaiʻi
cases.recognition: Apology Resolution of 1993; no recognition as a state
cases.story: The Hawaiian sovereignty movement seeks some form of self-government or an independent nation for Hawaii, and often redress for the 1893 overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani and the 1898 annexation, which it regards as illegal. In 1993 the US Congress passed the Apology Resolution, acknowledging the overthrow was illegal. Groups differ. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi, started in 1987 with Mililani Trask as first governor, has a constitution and elected officers and reported 21,000 members in 1997. In 1993 it led 10,000 people on a march to Iolani Palace. The Nation of Hawaiʻi, led by Dennis "Bumpy" Kanahele, wants a republic. It occupied the area around Makapuʻu lighthouse in 1989 and Kaupo Beach in 1993, and ended that occupation in exchange for land. The Akaka Bill, proposed in 2000, would begin federal recognition of a Native Hawaiian government. Many sovereignty groups oppose it, and a 2005 Grassroot Institute poll found most Hawaii residents opposed it too.
cases.mechanism: A government's apology for an illegal act does not itself restore sovereignty or return land.

cases.name: Central Tibetan Administration
cases.passports: Green Book, a contribution record also called the Tibetan-in-exile passport
cases.laws: Charter of the Tibetans in Exile
cases.recognition: No country recognises it as sovereign
cases.story: The Central Tibetan Administration is the government in exile of Tibet, based in Dharamshala, India. The 14th Dalai Lama rejected the 1951 17 Point Agreement with China in March 1959 as he fled to India, and re-established his cabinet, the Kashag, in exile on 29 April 1959. It has judicial, legislative and executive branches. Its charter was adopted in 1991, and in 2011 the Dalai Lama gave up political duties, leaving executive power with an elected leader called the Sikyong, currently Penpa Tsering. Tibetans abroad vote for the parliament and Sikyong and make annual contributions recorded in the Green Book, sometimes called a passport. Funding comes mainly from private donations, the Green Book and aid from governments such as India and the United States. No country recognises it as a sovereign government, although it receives financial aid for welfare work. Tibet was a founding member of the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization in 1991.
cases.mechanism: An exile government can hold elections and collect contributions without any territory, while recognition stays out of reach.

cases.name: Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic
cases.recognition: None found on the retrieved page
cases.story: The Rada was the representative body of the Belarusian People's Republic, proclaimed in Minsk in March 1918 under German occupation. On 25 March it declared independence and asked for international recognition. Its authority was limited by the occupation, and when Soviet forces advanced at the end of 1918 it moved from Minsk to Grodno. It has been in exile since 1919, kept alive among the Belarusian diaspora in the United States, Canada, Britain and Estonia, where it works as an advocacy group for independence and democracy. Ivonka Survilla has been its president since 1997. As of 2026 Wikipedia describes it as the oldest existing government in exile. During the 2020–2021 protests in Belarus it expressed support for Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya. It has held no territory for over a century.
cases.mechanism: A government in exile can survive for more than a century as an organisation, holding no land.
